title: CDC — Measles Cases and Outbreaks (United States)

chunks.text:
Source: https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html (data feed https://www.cdc.gov/wcms/vizdata/measles/measles_hosp.json), retrieved 2026-08-11.
As of the latest CDC update, a total of 2,465 confirmed measles cases were reported in the United States in 2026. There have been 0 confirmed deaths from measles in 2026.
As of the latest CDC update, a total of 2,289 confirmed measles cases were reported in the United States in 2025. There were 3 confirmed deaths from measles in 2025.
Note: this custom scraper renders the CDC measles JSON data feed into compact HTML because the page's case/death figures are injected client-side and are absent from the statically served table cells. Counts are cumulative year-to-date totals.

Measles is a highly contagious viral disease, which affects mostly children. It is transmitted via droplets from the nose, mouth, or throat of infected persons. Initial symptoms, which usually appear 10-12 days after infection, include high fever, runny nose, bloodshot eyes, and tiny white spots on the inside of the mouth. Several days later, a rash develops, starting on the face and upper neck and gradually spreading downwards.
There is no specific treatment for measles and most people recover within 2-3 weeks. However, particularly in malnourished children and people with reduced immunity, measles can cause serious complications, including blindness, encephalitis, severe diarrhea, ear infection, and pneumonia. Measles can be prevented by immunization.
• Measles is a very contagious viral disease that especially affects children and can cause severe health problems, including severe diarrhea, ear infections, blindness, pneumonia, and encephalitis (swelling of the brain). Some of these complications can lead to death.
• At the global level, measles continues to be one of the leading causes of death among young children, despite the fact that there is a safe and effective vaccine to prevent it. There is no specific antiviral treatment against the measles virus.
• Serious cases are especially frequent in malnourished young children, especially those whose immune systems are weakened. In populations with high levels of malnutrition and inadequate health care, measles can kill in up to 10% of cases.
• Measles is transmitted by airborne droplets from the nose, mouth, or throat of an infected person. The virus can stay active and contagious in the air or on surfaces for two hours.
• Symptoms tend to be high fever, runny nose, cough, red and watery eyes, small white spots on the inside of the cheeks, and widespread rash all over the body.
• Before widespread vaccination began in 1980, measles caused 2.6 million deaths a year throughout the world, 12,000 of them in the Americas.
• Between 1970 and 1979, Latin American countries reported about 220,000 cases of measles a year.

title: Measles cases reach 35-year high in US

chunks.text:
It’s only July, but the United States has already recorded 2,295 measles cases this year, a number not seen since 1991, according to new data published on the Johns Hopkins University measles tracker.
In 1991, the United States tracked 2,126 measles cases after recording 9,643 measles cases the prior year. A total of 2,289 confirmed measles cases were recorded in all of 2025, at least 700 of them associated with a large West Texas outbreak that killed two children. In October 2025, a massive measles outbreak began in South Carolina and continued until April of this year. That outbreak involved 997 confirmed cases and at least 21 hospitalizations.
The sustained transmission reported in the United States in the last two years puts the country’s elimination status in jeopardy per the Pan American Health Organization and is a sign that many communities have vaccination rates much lower than the 95% coverage needed for herd immunity.
Reaching this milestone is particularly striking because we are only in July.
“Reaching this milestone is particularly striking because we are only in July, and measles cases are still being reported throughout the country, with outbreaks in Virginia and Pennsylvania,” said William Moss, MD, MPH, a pediatric infectious disease epidemiologist and professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, in a statement to the press. “We urgently need to address the reasons for under-vaccination in some of our communities, particularly the disinformation that leads to mistrust of measles vaccines.”

While measles can be deadly, no one has died in the United States so far this year from the virus. But measles can cause a host of other medical maladies. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about 20% of unvaccinated Americans who get measles is hospitalized, with 1 in 20 developing pneumonia.
Ten percent of all US case-patients ages 5 and under this year have required hospitalization, as have 10% of those 20 years and older.
Last week, Utah officials published new data in a Public Health Alerts report describing outcomes among measles patients. The state has been battling an outbreak for 12 months involving 711 cases in the past 12 months, 514 of them in 2026 alone.
Only about 8% of patients in the current outbreak have been hospitalized, and of those, 90% were unvaccinated. Three of the five hospitalized patients who were vaccinated had "severe immunocompromising conditions.”
About 75% of hospitalized patients required intravenous infusions, and more than 60% needed supplemental oxygen, with 29% developing measles pneumonia. No cases of measles encephalitis, or brain swelling, were reported.
The data echoes a report of similar findings from South Carolina published last week, which showed no deaths but two cases of measles encephalitis among 81 patients, of whom 13 were hospitalized.

title: These states are hot spots for 2026's record measles outbreak

chunks.text:
Seven states account for the majority of measles cases in the United States, becoming hot spots for the life-threatening disease.
Why it matters: The U.S. measles case count has officiallyshattered last year's record — hitting levels unseen in more than three decades, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention datareleased Friday.
A Johns Hopkins University tracker that compiles state and local health data signaled the new record earlier this week.
The latest: As of late July, the CDC had recorded 2,318 cases for the year. The vast majority of those sickened are under 20 years old and are either unvaccinated or their status is unknown. There have been no recorded deaths.
Measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. some 26 years ago, thanks to an effective vaccination program.
When more than 95% of people are vaccinated in a community, most people are protected — but vaccination coverage among kindergarteners has slipped.
Yes, but:Sustained outbreaks over the past two years signal that the virus is finding new footing in areas with low vaccine coverage.
Where measles is hitting hardest
By the numbers: Two states dominate the national count of cases, according to CDC data.
South Carolina has reported 670 cases, while Utah has reported 522 cases. Together, they account for 1,192 cases, which is about 51% of the total.
Seven states — South Carolina, Utah, Texas, Virginia, Florida, Pennsylvania and Arizona — represent more than 84% of the total.
Yes, but: Twenty-three states — plus D.C. — have seen three or fewer cases, per the CDC.
Here's a look at the states with the highest cases.
South Carolina
South Carolina has had 670 cases this year, according to the CDC. In 2025, the state had 333 cases.
There was only one documented case in 2024, per the CDC.
In April, the state declared the end of a massive outbreak that totaled nearly 1,000 cases, most of which were in unvaccinated people, between October and March.
Utah
Utah had 197 cases in 2025. In 2026, the Beehive State has seen more than 500 cases.
In Utah, complications related to measles have ranged from pneumonia and dehydration to sepsis and shock, Axios' Erin Alberty writes.
Texas
Texas had 803 cases in 2025 — more than any other state — but has seen far fewer this year, with the state reporting 188 in 2026.
Vaccination rates for children have been dropping in Texas, just like the rest of the country.
Virginia
Virginia had only six cases in 2025, but has now seen 176 in 2026.
Cases have been climbing in Virginia all year, with officials pointing to the lack of vaccinations as a reason for the outbreaks.
Health officials are tracking a confirmed outbreak in two counties, Buckingham and Cumberland.
Florida
Florida has seen 141 cases in 2026 after only seeing eight cases in 2025 and 11 in 2025, per the CDC.
The Sunshine State saw a surge of cases earlier in the year, but there were signs that the state's outbreaks were slowing down.
Pennsylvania
Pennsylvania has seen a surge of cases over the last week, rising from 110 to 134 — the biggest share of upticks in CDC data this week.
Arizona
Arizona saw the second biggest increase in cases over the last week, jumping by nine cases to a 108 total for the year.
